evidence: ProjectController.ts, TaskController.ts and UserController.ts each declare a class with constructor-injected use cases and a routes(): Router method, so they share one consistent adapter shape.

Every body-parsing handler uses readBody/requiredString from '../RequestParsing' (ProjectController.create/addTask, TaskController.assign, UserController.create). TaskController.complete only reads req.params.taskId.
ProjectController.addTask is the only caller of CreateTaskUseCase, mounted at POST /projects/:projectId/tasks, so the logic is not duplicated in TaskController.
ProjectController.ts defines a local queryString(req, field) that throws BadRequestError from RequestParsing. It is used only in listTasks and not duplicated elsewhere.
Status codes are consistent: res.status(201) for create endpoints and the default 200 res.json for the rest.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: All three controllers serve a single concern: they adapt HTTP requests (via an Express Router) to application use cases. They share an identical structure: constructor-injected use cases, a routes(): Router method, and handlers that parse the request, call execute and return JSON. Each body-parsing handler uses the shared readBody/requiredString helpers from ../RequestParsing, and ProjectController.addTask also uses optionalString. TaskController.complete only reads a path parameter. Resources are split cleanly: ProjectController owns /projects and its nested /projects/:projectId/tasks routes, TaskController owns /tasks/:taskId/*, and UserController owns /users. Task creation sits only under the nested project route, so it is not duplicated. The one local helper, queryString in ProjectController.ts, reuses BadRequestError from RequestParsing and appears nowhere else, so no rule or invariant is duplicated. It could later move into RequestParsing if other controllers need query parsing, but today it is not a bypass of the module's abstractions.
